title: Jewish humor
hook: laughter as a way of surviving

segments.voice: Yesterday, interfaith families, and your line: families are complex. These last days were about who belongs: Jews by choice, every face, cultural Jews, families with two traditions. The week ends with a laugh.

A man is rescued after years alone on a desert island. His rescuers find he's built himself two synagogues. Why two, they ask. He points. This one I go to. That one, I wouldn't set foot in. People tell that joke at Jewish tables, about themselves. It's warm, a little sharp, and true enough to sting. It also hides something serious. A people that lived through exile, expulsions and grief kept something in its pocket the whole time: the ability to laugh, including at itself.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES ON ONE ISLAND.` → `A JOKE TOLD ABOUT OURSELVES.` → `LAUGHTER KEPT IN THE POCKET.`

segments.voice: Laughter shows up early in the Torah, in an unexpected place. Sarah, old and long past hoping, overhears a visitor tell Abraham she'll have a son. She laughs to herself. When the child is born, she says God has made laughter for her, and everyone who hears will laugh with her. The boy is named Yitzchak, Isaac, and readers have long heard laughter in that name: a promise so unlikely the only honest answer was to laugh. The Psalms remember laughter at the other end of a hard road. A psalm about coming home from captivity says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter." Not after everything was fixed. At the moment of return, still dusty. And the Talmud tells a small, lovely story. A rabbi named Beroka stands in a crowded market with the prophet Elijah and asks: is anyone here destined for the world to come? Elijah points to two ordinary men. The rabbi asks what they do. We're jesters, they say. When we see someone sad, we cheer them up. When we see two people quarreling, we work to make peace between them. In that whole crowded market, they're among the very few Elijah points to. In this tradition, humor at its best isn't a way of hiding from pain. It's a way of carrying it, and of carrying each other. A joke can let a frightened room breathe. It can puncture the pompous and spare the weak. It can say, we're still here.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` · `THEN WAS OUR MOUTH FILLED WITH LAUGHTER.` · `TWO JESTERS IN THE MARKET.` · `HUMOR THAT CARRIES PAIN.` · then, large: `LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Go looking in memory for something that made you laugh: a family story, a line a friend said, something a child got gloriously wrong. Choose one that makes nobody smaller, and notice what it does to your face just to remember it. Then think of one person who could use it, someone tired or sad, the way the jesters in the market carried theirs.
Jewish humor. Laughter carried through hard times, aimed at life and at oneself, and honored in the Talmud's story of the two jesters. Today's word.
Your line: laugh. A good laugh can carry a lot. That's the week, and day one thousand fifty.

howItsDone: Jewish humor lives in family stories, folk tales, Yiddish and Ladino sayings, holiday spoofs such as Purim plays, and in writers and comedians, and it is often told by Jews about themselves.

chat.says: Why do so many Jewish jokes poke fun at Jews themselves? Isn't that odd?
options: It's a way of carrying pain and each other; the Talmud even praises two jesters.
It began as a way to mock the rabbis and their strict rules about prayer.
It's mostly a way to hide from pain, so nobody has to talk about it.
chat.meaning: In this tradition humor at its best carries pain rather than hiding it; in the Talmud, Elijah points to two jesters who cheer people and make peace.
